📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mo Brings Plenty, his family and community have been rocked by the untimely death of Mo’s nephew, 1923 actor Cole Brings Plenty. The 27-year-old was found dead in April 2024 after he had been reported missing. His death came between seasons one and two of the Yellowstone prequel, sparking his recasting (with Jeremy Gauna), a final season that honored his memory and now, an entire episode of Marshals inspired by what happened.

According to recent reports, in Sunday’s episode of Yellowstone‘s hit CBS spinoff following Kayce Dutton (Luke Grimes), titled “Roughstock,” Mo, an enrolled member of the Lakota Nations who plays the right-hand man to Broken Rock Tribe chief Thomas Rainwater (Gil Birmingham) in both Yellowstone and Marshals, searches on horseback with Kayce (Grimes) for Mo’s missing nephew (played by Will Strongheart), only to eventually find him dead, and a police department refusing to investigate the death. Related Stories TV Michelle Pfeiffer and Kurt Russell Tease Major "Twists" in Season 2 of 'The Madison' TV Luke Grimes Wasn't Sure If 'Marshals' Would Be a Hit. Now He's Prepping for a 'Yellowstone' Kind of Run.

In a recent development, the storyline is ripped from what Mo believes happened to his real nephew. In Cole’s case, the Lawrence Police Department in Kansas found no foul play involved, ruling that Cole acted alone and took his own life. Mo hasn’t stopped pushing a different narrative ever since. “For his murder to go uninvestigated, and for it to be written off as ‘no foul play,’ because they didn’t want to invest anything into it? It’s heartbreaking,” he had told The Hollywood Reporter back in March. “We’re not letting it go.”.

Now that the episode has aired, Mo, who also works behind the scenes as the show’s American Indian Affairs coordinator, talks again with THR below about the bravery of the Paramount Taylor Sheridan series and Marshals showrunner Spencer Hudnut to spotlight Cole’s story on television, the emotions around reliving the tragedy of his nephew’s death, and the justice he hopes the episode can help bring to murdered and missing Indigenous people. “This is for the injustice that occurs to American Indian people and the victims who are truly victims, who are being being labeled otherwise and not being taken seriously,” he claims.

Industry observers note that this must be heavy for you, so thank you for speaking with me about the making of this episode inspired by your late nephew. Did you approach (showrunner) Spencer Hudnut about doing this, or did Spencer approach you?

It all began when my brother, Joe, Cole’s father, and I were sharing the experience of what we were going through. Spencer mentioned something about it being up to us. Saying, “I know it’s gonna be deep, and it’s hard. But it’s up to you.” We stated, we have to do it. Not just for the sake of remembrance or in honoring Cole, but for all the other cases, all the other families whose cases of their loved ones not being looked at or being taken seriously and just thrown away. It was very notable. And I knew it was going to be doable because the cast and crew are an amazing group of people. They all understood and had the knowledge of what we’ve experienced and gone through.

Did you have to pitch this to the studio or network to get them on board?

Sources indicate that I think that was on Spencer. Mad respect for Spencer; even doing so, is very important.

Did you talk to Taylor Sheridan about how to handle putting this storyline into the show?

No. I knew exactly what I wanted to do. My biggest thing was that I wanted to relay the true emotions and spirit of it all, even the frustrating moments. Because it’s a roller coaster ride, and it still is today. It’s still fresh in our minds, my family’s minds, especially my brother Joel. He struggled. It was truly, truly a great loss for us.

Industry observers note that spencer wrote this episode. Did you collaborate?

Yes, he wrote it, and Spencer and the writing team are a great group of amazing, beautiful human beings. My brother and I went to the writers room early on, before the season even started, to spend a day with them. We talked about different things that go on within tribal councils, the political side of what goes on on a reservation, the non-political side of it and then, of course, we shared our experience of not talking about the MMIW (Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women) and MMIP (Missing and Murdered Indigenous People), but actually conveying what it’s really like to have that experience. There are hundreds and hundreds of families who have their loved ones… murdered and missing; the disappearance of loved ones just being written off as nothing.

According to recent reports, from my previous conversations with you, this episode is very close to what you believe happened to your nephew in real life. What was it like for you to film this beat by beat, playing an uncle who loses his nephew? [Note: In the end of the episode, Kayce’s team pushes for the police to investigate the death, opening up the storyline to continue.].

It was about doing justice. But it was also good to have Luke Grimes there, and Gil Birmingham, and the crew; individuals who understood and knew. Will [Strongheart], who portrayed [Mo’s onscreen nephew] Troy, was very familiar. He came to Cole’s funeral; they all knew what we were going through, especially for me. So it was easy to fall back into that space, because I knew there were others who would be there to help me if I needed it. But at the forefront of my mind was the injustice that occurs to American Indian people and the victims who are truly victims who are being being labeled otherwise and not being taken seriously.

This is a significant platform: Marshals is a mega-hit for Paramount. You will shine a light on this happening everywhere, but do you hope it moves the needle specifically with your nephew’s case?

Unfortunately, the way I see it, if a police department doesn’t want to investigate something then there’s a connection. Bottom line, hands down. Outside of that, what I hope this episode achieves is that it will drive people who are non-Native, who are unfamiliar, to go down this journey.

We mentioned MMIW, MMIP, in the past — murdered and missing Indian women and people. But to actually have a storyline that will hopefully have the audience see it through Mo’s, Kayce’s, Rainwater’s eyes? Just to be able to actually see what is going on. The positive side in this story is that law enforcement actually does get involved — the marshals, but not the police. There’s a line where the sheriff stated, “Ah, this happens all the time.” I’m glad Spencer included that line because that’s really, honestly, what a lot of families hear from law enforcement when when their loved ones are found.

It has been revealed that after we spoke the last time, the Lawrence Police Department responded to our interview with a statement. Did you see what they remarked? [“The entire case contains clear evidence that there was no foul play involved in Cole’s death and that Cole acted alone.”].

In a recent development, oh, yeah, of course. Out of respect for my family, I encouraged my brother, Joe, to seal the records. Little did we know that it was going to give them an out. Nonetheless, I’m hoping that this episode is going to drive people to reach out to their Congress people, their senators, their governors, and say, “Hey, look, enough. Here’s the original inhabitants of this country, and here’s our treatment to them.”.

Industry observers note that but yet we speak about other nationalities in foreign countries, so we’re basically flying over mission fields to get to mission fields. We want to be the savior there, but we’re not doing it here. That’s the thing that upsets me the most, and the fact that we are tax paying people as well. First responders get their funding through tax dollars. We are forced to pay taxes, and the will of justice does not turn for us? Shame on America for that. I’m being honest. And if that’s the case, then we shouldn’t have to pay taxes. If there’s no equality and justice being served for our loved ones who are truly victimized?

In a recent development, what occurred in Cole’s case, there were allegations. And they let go the people they should have interviewed to get the true answers. If the police department really doesn’t want to investigate, then to me, that’s every bit of proof that there’s something to hide.

This episode included a ceremonial burial. You have worked behind the scenes to bring authenticity to this franchise for years as the American Indian Affairs coordinator. What did you especially want to show here as Mo was laying his nephew to rest?

Sources indicate that the sacred fire… the true celebration and understanding of life. When we look at life from a spiritual perspective, it is continuous. There is no end. So that was vital, because we incorporate a lot of that understanding or tradition or ceremony into our everyday lives, whether we’re assisting a family that lost a loved one or, or even ourselves, losing relatives. The spirit is forever.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest parts of that ceremony scene was the horse. Because we’ve always had horses here in this country long before the Spanish brought theirs. The Lakota people, we have songs and ceremonies specifically for the horse that are thousands upon thousands of years old, so to have that incorporated was very vital to me. To share that bit of knowledge and understanding that our people have always had, that the horse symbolizes the spiritual realm. So when Mo sees that horse, he knows his nephew made it home.

Is there anything you want to say about Cole in his memory?

If people truly believe there’s a higher power, then they have to stand up for what’s right. Regardless of what it is. My nephew, Cole, has always done that. He was a lover of life. He always gave a helping hand. He never judged anyone for who they were, what nationality, what their faith was. If someone needed help, he was there. And to turn that type of light out in a community, in this world… for us, he was the next one to carry on our traditions and knowledge. To strip us of that and do nothing about it? If people truly believe in a higher power, they better understand and know that it is the higher power who loves diversity. Because the higher power made it so from the very beginning. And if you can’t support that diversity here, this world, on this planet, then who are you to believe you’ll be welcome there?

In Marshals, the death of Mo’s nephew sounds like an ongoing story that will open up the show to explore more reservation stories, which is something Spencer Hednut mentioned is baked into the series.

According to recent reports, there are many stories very similar to this. Different situations and circumstances, but the outcome’s always the same. I wanted to get this message out but I had to utilize our own story, my family’s own experience. I’m hoping down the road this will give us the ability for us to be able to share more; other things that are occurring. Not always the negative things. There are positive things as well, and I want to share those too. I’m hoping people will go ahead and support stories about Indian country.

Do you feel like this was a brave thing by the show, the network, the studio to allow you to tell such a personal story?

Recent findings suggest that I’m thankful to the network for giving us the opportunity. I’m thankful to the Spencer. I’m thankful that they’ve allowed us to be able to share this experience and bring it to light through the episodes. It does take great courage, because a lot of people don’t understand cultural diversity. They don’t fully understand that we as American Indian people are tax paying people, too. Like I mentioned, we pay bills just like everyone else. We have to work for everything that we have. I’m thankful to the network and to Spencer and to the rest of the writers who supported the whole storyline.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore.

Latest Update: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after more than 40 years of searching, physicists at CERN have reached a major milestone in their hunt for one of the rarest known particle decays.
  • The finding, declared during a seminar at CERN, marks the first time a single experiment has produced sufficient evidence for this extraordinarily rare event.
  • Recent findings suggest that at the center of the discovery is a particle called Bd, which contains a beauty quark and a down antiquark.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after more than 40 years of searching, physicists at CERN have reached a major milestone in their hunt for one of the rarest known particle decays. Researchers working with the LHCb experiment have detected evidence of a process expected to occur only once in approximately 10 billion beauty particle decays.

The finding, declared during a seminar at CERN, marks the first time a single experiment has produced sufficient evidence for this extraordinarily rare event. Beyond its rarity, the decay is particularly valuable because it could help scientists investigate particles that are too massive to be created directly in the Large Hadron Collider.

Recent findings suggest that at the center of the discovery is a particle called Bd, which contains a beauty quark and a down antiquark. Scientists found evidence that this particle can decay into a pair of muons (μ+μ-). Muons are similar to electrons but have greater mass. The results agree with predictions from the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions, and help narrow the possibilities for upcoming particles beyond it.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal Newly introduced Physics.

Recent findings suggest that one reason physicists are so interested in these unusual decays is that quantum effects allow other particles to influence how they occur. Even particles too heavy to be produced in the Large Hadron Collider can potentially leave subtle traces in the rates of these processes.

Sources indicate that by measuring extremely rare decays with high precision, researchers can look for differences between experimental results and theoretical predictions. Such discrepancies could provide indirect evidence of previously unknown particles. Generally, the rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to these hidden influences.

The decay known as Bd → μ+μ-belongs to a special category that physicists have long considered 'golden channels' for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model. During this process, a beauty quark and an antiquark with the opposite electric charge annihilate each other. Their energy is transformed into a muon and its antiparticle.

Recent findings suggest that scientists have previously observed a related process involving a different beauty particle, called Bs. In 2015, a joint analysis by the LHCb and CMS collaborations reported the first confirmed observation of Bs → μ+μ-, along with initial evidence for the much rarer Bd decay.

However, subsequent analyses incorporating data collected through 2018 could not confirm the earlier evidence for Bd → μ+μ-. The difference in rarity is substantial. The Bs decay occurs approximately three times per billion beauty particle decays, while the Bd process is predicted to happen about 30 times less frequently.

Upgraded CERN Detector Makes the Breakthrough Possible.

A significant improvement to the LHCb experiment helped researchers overcome the enormous difficulty of detecting such a rare event.

Following a major upgrade, the experiment began collecting data in 2024 at five times the rate achieved between 2010 and 2018. The upgraded detector also became better at identifying different kinds of particles, giving researchers a clearer picture of the activity produced during collisions.

The team combined these improvements with machine learning techniques to distinguish the exceptionally rare signals from the vast number of other particle processes. Without these advances, the events scientists wanted to study would have been overwhelmed by the background.

It has been revealed that "Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than forty years," remarked Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team of 19 scientists. "Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background.".

Four Decades of Searching Finally Produce Strong Evidence.

In particle physics, scientists use a statistical measure called standard deviations to evaluate how likely an apparent signal is to result from random fluctuations rather than a genuine physical process.

Industry observers note that A result must reach three standard deviations to qualify as evidence of a latest phenomenon. At that level, the probability of random fluctuations producing a signal at least as statistically extreme is approximately 0.3%.

Using data collected during 2024 and 2025, the LHCb researchers identified evidence of Bd → μ+μ- at a significance of 3.0 standard deviations. When they combined those measurements with earlier data gathered between 2011 and 2018, the statistical significance increased to 3.2 standard deviations, exceeding the widely accepted threshold for evidence.

The same investigation also produced the most precise measurements ever obtained for the related Bs → μ+μ-decay, providing additional information about these exceptionally uncommon processes.

Sources indicate that although the new findings represent a major achievement, physicists have not yet reached the threshold required to declare a confirmed observation. That milestone requires a significance of five standard deviations.

If future measurements achieve that level of certainty, Bd → μ+μ-would become the rarest beauty particle decay ever observed.

Future Large Hadron Collider Upgrades Could Uncover Hidden Particles.

Researchers expect upcoming improvements to the Large Hadron Collider to make these measurements even more powerful.

Industry observers note that the High Luminosity LHC, also known as the HiLumi LHC, is scheduled to begin operating in 2030. Another major upgrade to the LHCb experiment is planned for the middle of the following decade. Together, these developments could eventually increase the experiment's data collection rate by another factor of ten.

Sources indicate that collecting much larger datasets would allow physicists to detect more of these extremely rare decays and measure their properties with greater precision. That increased sensitivity could make it possible to identify subtle effects associated with particles that remain beyond the direct reach of existing accelerators.

"Seeing evidence of this rare decay is incredibly exciting, opening up latest possibilities to probe beyond the direct reach of the LHC," explained Harry Cliff, LHCb's Rare Decays Convener and Analysis Co-lead.

"The future LHCb upgrade will allow us to observe many more of these decays, providing even greater sensitivity to undiscovered particles.".

For physicists who have pursued this elusive signal for more than four decades, the new evidence represents a long-awaited advance. It also offers a promising way to investigate whether the known laws of particle physics are part of a much larger picture.

Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand.
  • Sources indicate that I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see.
  • In a recent development, this is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand.

Sources indicate that I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again.

In a recent development, this is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky.

The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up.

Recent findings suggest that but every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that the Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns.

In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun, but their stars are about 625 million years old.

The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Major Dipper/Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness.

In a recent development, that makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them.

I'm going to run my Pleiades eye test in stages. First, I'll step outside and look almost immediately. I'll count the individual stars I can distinguish without spending ages convincing myself about marginal ones. Then I'll wait. After about 10 minutes (without looking at my phone or bright outdoor lights, of course), I'll count again. Full dark adaptation takes considerably longer, but even 10 minutes can make an obvious difference when you've just come from a brightly lit house.

Industry observers note that I'll then try my trusty 10x50 binoculars. This is where the experiment stops being subtle. The little naked-eye knot of brightness suddenly becomes a field filled with stars. The Pleiades don't just become brighter through binoculars. Their whole character changes because stars that were below my naked-eye threshold appear. I'll also use the averted vision technique, looking slightly to one side rather than directly at M45. It's one of the best demonstrations of the technique, with its fainter stars seemingly popping into view as your more light-sensitive peripheral vision takes over.

The moon is returning to the evening sky this week, waxing from a thin crescent toward first quarter. It reaches first quarter around Nov. 17, so moonlight becomes progressively more noticeable during the first half of the night. Look southwest during twilight, and you'll see the beautiful sight of a crescent moon sporting Earthshine, sunlight reflected from Earth onto the moon's night side.

According to recent reports, overnight, Nov. 15-16, don't miss Mars and Jupiter in conjunction. The two planets will appear just over a degree apart, rising in the east during the evening before climbing high into the southern sky in the hours before sunrise.

The following night, Nov. 17-18, the Leonid meteor shower peaks. This is one shower where staying up later actually matters. Leo, the constellation containing the shower's radiant, doesn't rise until late, so the better opportunity comes after midnight and toward the predawn hours.

Auriga, "the Charioteer," is easy to see in the northeastern and eastern sky during November evenings, but have you spied the asterism close to its brightest star, Capella? It's known as the "Goat Star," though its Latin name is the diminutive of capra, meaning "little she-goat." The reason is esoteric — Capella represents Amalthea, the mythological goat that suckled the infant Zeus — but there is a neat asterism (shape of stars) nearby that suddenly makes sense. Close to Capella is a triangle of faint stars that are known as The Kids — Epsilon, Zeta and Eta Aurigae — traditionally imagined as the offspring of Capella. It's one of those little patterns that makes a constellation much easier to recognize.

NASA reveals bold new strategy to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that NASA has revealed new details about its accelerated effort to return American astronauts to the Moon in 2028.
  • During an October 23 briefing, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders outlined the next steps for the Artemis program.
  • Industry observers note that the announcement builds on priorities introduced earlier this year through NASA's Ignition initiative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that NASA has revealed new details about its accelerated effort to return American astronauts to the Moon in 2028. The updated strategy includes testing two competing lunar landers, streamlining rocket preparations, and introducing a lighter spacesuit to help make the first moonwalks possible sooner.

During an October 23 briefing, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders outlined the next steps for the Artemis program. The revised approach centers on two major missions: Artemis III, a test flight scheduled for 2027, and Artemis IV, which is intended to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

Industry observers note that the announcement builds on priorities introduced earlier this year through NASA's Ignition initiative. Agency officials also highlighted recent progress in spacecraft development, mission preparations, and partnerships with private aerospace companies. These efforts are intended to reduce technical risks, accelerate the schedule, and establish the foundation for a lasting American presence on the Moon.

According to recent reports, "This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story. We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible," remarked Isaacman. "NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we're not waiting for others to bring their prepares to us -- the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth.".

Artemis III Will Test Two Lunar Landers in Earth Orbit.

In a recent development, before attempting another crewed Moon landing, NASA looks to conduct a major rehearsal in Earth orbit. The Artemis III mission will bring together NASA's Orion spacecraft and experimental lunar landers developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin.

Four astronauts will travel aboard Orion, launching on NASA's powerful SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. During the planned 14-day mission, the crew will practice rendezvous and docking procedures with both companies' lander test vehicles. Rendezvous involves guiding two spacecraft to meet in orbit, while docking allows them to connect so astronauts can move between vehicles.

These demonstrations are designed to verify important spacecraft capabilities before Artemis IV attempts to carry astronauts to the Moon's surface.

In a recent development, the tests will take place in a carefully planned sequence. Blue Origin will first launch a test version of its Blue Moon lander into Earth orbit. NASA will then send Orion and its four astronauts into space aboard the SLS rocket, where Orion will rendezvous and dock with the Blue Moon vehicle.

Next, SpaceX will launch a test version of its Version 3 Starship lunar lander. Orion will separate from Blue Moon and perform another docking maneuver, this time with Starship. By testing both systems during a single crewed mission, NASA aims to gather essential operational experience while reducing uncertainties before the 2028 landing attempt.

NASA Cuts Rocket Preparation Times and Costs.

The new mission details follow other recent Artemis progress reports. According to NASA, the hardware needed for Artemis III remains on schedule, and improvements in processing have reduced preparation timelines by approximately 50%.

The agency also reported a significant engineering achievement involving a critical rocket fuel-line component. Rather than relying on an outside supplier, NASA engineers redesigned, manufactured, and tested the component themselves in just five months. The work cost roughly one-tenth of an earlier estimate from an external vendor.

It has been revealed that "NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it," noted Jeremy Parsons, the agency's Artemis program manager. "It's an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise.".

The improvements reflect NASA's broader effort to strengthen its internal engineering capabilities, shorten development schedules, and reduce the cost of preparing missions for launch.

SpaceX and Blue Origin Offer Different Paths to the Moon.

In a recent development, for Artemis IV in 2028, NASA intends to launch astronauts aboard Orion using the SLS rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Once in space, the crew will rely on a lunar landing system developed by either SpaceX or Blue Origin to reach the Moon's surface.

Sources indicate that both companies have revised their original mission designs to make operations simpler, more efficient, and more adaptable. Although they share the same objective, their approaches to transporting astronauts to the lunar surface differ considerably.

SpaceX aims to use its Starship spacecraft, which will take on additional propellant while orbiting Earth. After refueling, Starship will meet Orion and carry the spacecraft toward the Moon. Refueling in orbit is an important part of SpaceX's strategy because it allows the vehicle to receive the propellant needed for its journey after leaving the launchpad.

Blue Origin is developing a different approach using its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander. Its strategy calls for additional propulsion stages in Earth orbit to send the lander toward the Moon. The lander will then meet Orion in a relatively low lunar orbit before carrying astronauts down to the surface.

Both companies are working toward having their systems ready to support a crewed Moon landing in 2028. Maintaining two potential landing systems gives NASA greater flexibility as development and testing continue.

NASA Explores Newly introduced Rocket Options for Artemis IV.

Industry observers note that NASA is also considering two possible upper stages for the SLS rocket used on Artemis IV. An upper stage is the portion of a rocket that provides additional propulsion after the earlier stages have completed their work, helping send a spacecraft toward its destination.

One option is the interim cryogenic propulsion stage already used by SLS. The other is an extended version of United Launch Alliance's Centaur V upper stage, which would hold additional propellant.

By developing both possibilities, NASA hopes to preserve flexibility in its launch plans and avoid becoming dependent on a single technical solution. Having alternatives could help the agency respond to engineering challenges without jeopardizing the broader Moon landing schedule.

A Upcoming Lightweight Spacesuit Could Speed Up Moonwalks.

Another key change involves the spacesuits astronauts will wear while exploring the lunar surface.

NASA is working with Axiom Space on a second, lighter design known as the "Sortie suit." The latest suit is intended specifically for the first Moon surface excursions and weighs approximately half as much as Axiom's larger primary spacesuit.

The lighter design could simplify preparations for the earliest landing missions and help astronauts begin exploring the lunar surface sooner.

Industry observers note that however, the Sortie suit is not intended to replace the primary design. Axiom's more capable suit will remain part of NASA's prepares for future missions that require longer periods outside the spacecraft and more demanding surface activities.

Building a Permanent Human Presence on the Moon.

NASA's ambitions extend well beyond returning astronauts to the lunar surface for a single mission.

As the Artemis program advances, the agency intends to send crews on increasingly challenging expeditions near the Moon's South Pole. This region is an key focus of future lunar exploration, and the missions are designed to expand how much of the Moon humans can investigate directly.

Recent findings suggest that NASA describes the effort as part of a new Golden Age of innovation and exploration. The agency expects its lunar missions to support scientific discoveries, generate economic benefits, and encourage the development of technologies needed for more ambitious space exploration.

Ultimately, the goal is to establish an enduring human presence on the Moon rather than repeat the brief visits of earlier lunar expeditions. The experience gained from operating spacecraft, supporting astronauts, and carrying out increasingly complex missions on the lunar surface will also help NASA prepare for another historic objective: sending the first astronauts to Mars.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-upcoming Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov.
  • Sources indicate that after more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing.
  • "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-upcoming Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13).

Sources indicate that after more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour, sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall.

"It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

According to recent reports, "There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience.".

Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life.

There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with.

According to recent reports, as for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top.

You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you).

This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this fresh center has to offer.

According to recent reports, the new air and space center is designed for all ages, and for civilians and astronauts alike. For instance, looking at Endeavour spurred some memories for Reisman: He reflected on his time aboard the shuttle and his time as an astronaut and pinpointed specific places on the shuttle that played important roles in his mission.

It has been revealed that "I'm looking at handrails that I held onto during a spacewalk," he mentioned. "They're the same handrails. My hand was in the glove, but it was wrapped around those handrails. And I practiced for a long time exactly how I was going to do that, how I was going to root my tether, and all that kind of stuff. And I get to stand [here] now. When you go up the elevator there, you can actually have a direct view of those handrails, and every time I see that, I'm thinking about that spacewalk.".

Recent findings suggest that but you don't need to have completed a spacewalk to get that view. And, as of today, the general public is welcome to visit the museum, which is free to the public — as is the newly introduced aerospace center with its Endeavour exhibit.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers.
  • Industry observers note that in India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online.
  • According to recent reports, in France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.

Industry observers note that in India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.

According to recent reports, in France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.

Recent findings suggest that in both countries, the anger of the students demonstrates no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.

Recent findings suggest that it is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.

Recent findings suggest that the value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” stated Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”.

#622. Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant.
  • Industry observers note that scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an key part of the answer.
  • In a recent development, dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

Industry observers note that scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an key part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

In a recent development, dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

The new research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," mentioned Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

Sources indicate that the findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better.".

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain.

Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

In a recent development, when food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

It has been revealed that to investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

Sources indicate that the amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences.

In a recent development, finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

After mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments demonstrated that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain.

Industry observers note that the researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Recent findings suggest that identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

Recent findings suggest that one area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the fresh study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

It has been revealed that still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight stated.

The discovery offers a fresh perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

#619. 100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (video, photos)

100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (video, photos)

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite lifted off from Rocket Lab's Upcoming Zealand site on Saturday (Nov.
  • The mission, which Rocket Lab called "The Mountain God Rises," was a big one: It marked the 100th launch to date for the California-based company.
  • Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rocket Lab just hit the century mark.

Sources indicate that an Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite lifted off from Rocket Lab's Upcoming Zealand site on Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local New Zealand time).

The mission, which Rocket Lab called "The Mountain God Rises," was a big one: It marked the 100th launch to date for the California-based company.

Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018.

In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers.

And it hit the century mark on Saturday in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck.

In a recent development, "It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck said on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 rolls out.".

Electron met the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery.

"Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage.

Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE, which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date.

In a recent development, "The Mountain God Rises" was Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based manufacturer iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. And all went to initiative on the mission: Electron's upper "kick stage" deployed a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth.

SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 14 with news of successful liftoff, then again at 1:30 a.m. ET with news of satellite deployment.

#616. Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1879 w)

Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the first animals to make the transition from water to land nearly 380 million years ago may have had a surprising limitation: they could barely turn their heads.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery challenges a decades-old explanation for why animals developed distinct necks in the first place.
  • According to recent reports, to investigate this possibility, an international team of researchers combined fresh fossil evidence with experiments on living fish and computer models of ancient anatomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the first animals to make the transition from water to land nearly 380 million years ago may have had a surprising limitation: they could barely turn their heads. Although scientists have long believed that the evolution of necks gave these pioneering creatures greater freedom to look around, newly introduced research suggests their necks were actually remarkably stiff.

Sources indicate that the discovery challenges a decades-old explanation for why animals developed distinct necks in the first place. Rather than evolving to improve head movement, necks may have emerged as part of broader changes to the skeleton that allowed animals to use their front limbs for movement.

According to recent reports, to investigate this possibility, an international team of researchers combined fresh fossil evidence with experiments on living fish and computer models of ancient anatomy. Their findings, published October 14 in the journal Nature, offer a new perspective on one of the most vital evolutionary transitions in Earth's history.

"This is a really interesting time in Earth's history where some of the first forests are forming, and there's a really radical reorganization of the Earth," stated Tom Stewart, an assistant professor of biology at Penn State and a member of the research team. "So, understanding exactly when our lineage made that transition from water to land, how it was achieved, and which anatomical systems were changing is an important part of that story. What's cool is that many of the changes that were occurring in the skeleton at this time, about 380 million years ago, are still reflected in our own bodies today.".

Why Scientists Thought Animals Evolved Necks.

For decades, the prevailing explanation was that necks evolved to give early tetrapods, the ancestors of four-limbed vertebrates, greater control over their heads as they adapted to life outside the water.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. An animal living in shallow water or moving onto land would benefit from looking downward or turning its head from side to side to locate prey, recognize threats, and explore its surroundings. A flexible neck would allow it to do this without repositioning its entire body.

It has been revealed that modern fish generally lack a distinct neck because their shoulder structures connect directly to their skulls. To look in another direction, they typically have to turn their bodies instead. Separating the head from the shoulders therefore appeared to be an important step toward greater mobility.

However, determining how these ancient animals actually moved has been difficult. Much of their backbone consisted of soft tissue that rarely survives long enough to become fossilized, leaving scientists with an incomplete picture of how their necks functioned.

It has been revealed that "The fish that were undergoing these changes had a vertebral column that was largely made up of soft tissue, which, unlike bone, is rarely preserved in the fossil record," Stewart said. "In these cases, we can look to modern animals to serve as analogues for the past, like how living birds can teach us about now extinct dinosaurs.".

Ancient Fish Fossils Reveal a Turning Point in Evolution.

Some of the best evidence for the transition from water to land comes from fish that lived during the Devonian Period, approximately 420 to 360 million years ago.

These ancient animals possessed an unusual combination of features. While they retained many characteristics of aquatic fish, some had stronger, more substantial fins that may have helped support their weight. Such adaptations could have allowed them to lift themselves off the bottom or push through shallow water.

At the same time, certain species began showing a clear separation between the skull and shoulders, creating the first distinct necks.

Sources indicate that one especially notable example is Tiktaalik, a fossil fish first described in 2006. Its remains were discovered on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada, in the northern Arctic. Because Tiktaalik is closely related to the earliest vertebrates with limbs, its anatomy provides valuable clues about the evolutionary changes that eventually made life on land possible.

In a recent development, "Tiktaalik is one of these fossil fish, and it was first described in 2006," Stewart said. "It has been reasonably assumed for decades that this separation of head and shoulders must have allowed the head to move more freely, so the hypothesis that neck mobility was an evolutionary driver for this change in the tetrapod body proposal has prevailed, at least until now.".

Tiktaalik also helps researchers understand other major changes that occurred during this evolutionary transition, including the shift from drawing food into the mouth through suction underwater to biting on land, as well as the gradual transformation of swimming structures into limbs used for walking.

Industry observers note that "The materials have been really important because Tiktaalik is one of the closest relatives to limbed vertebrates," Stewart said. "It helps us to reconstruct a lot of intermediary steps in the transition to life on land, such as the move from suction feeding in water to biting on land or from swimming to walking.".

How Modern Sturgeon Helped Solve an Ancient Mystery.

The key to testing the traditional explanation for neck evolution came from an unexpected source: the sturgeon, a modern fish sometimes described as a living fossil because it retains several ancient anatomical features.

Recent findings suggest that early tetrapods had backbones that were very different from those of most vertebrates living today. Instead of relying primarily on a series of large vertebrae connected by joints, their spinal columns contained a prominent structure called the notochord.

The notochord is a long, flexible rod of tissue that runs through the vertebral column and helps support the body. In these ancient animals, the individual vertebrae were relatively small and arranged around a much larger tube of soft tissue.

Because this arrangement responds to forces differently from a modern backbone, researchers had struggled to determine how much flexibility it would have allowed. That uncertainty prevented them from directly testing the idea that necks initially evolved to improve head movement.

Sturgeon provided an opportunity to overcome that problem. Although they are only distantly related to the ancient animals being studied, their backbones have a similar notochord structure.

In a recent development, the research team measured the stiffness and mechanical properties of the notochord in modern sturgeon. They then incorporated those measurements into models of fossil animals, including early tetrapods such as Tiktaalik, to estimate how far their necks could actually move.

In a recent development, the results were striking. Even when the head and shoulders were anatomically separated, the structure of the backbone would have severely restricted movement. The earliest necks appear to have been much less flexible than researchers had assumed.

In a recent development, "We know that tetrapods did eventually gain higher neck mobility," noted Dana Korneisel, a postdoctoral researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden and first author of the paper. "Clearly it was advantageous eventually, but it was not an advantage available to these early tetrapods yet because of the limitations of their anatomy.".

The First Necks Were Surprisingly Stiff.

Sources indicate that the researchers had expected the upcoming models to clarify how much additional movement early necks provided. Instead, they found that most of the animals they examined would have gained little ability to reposition their heads.

According to recent reports, "I undertook this study to find out how big of a difference this change in anatomy made for these animals," Korneisel mentioned. "The vertebral columns of sturgeon are built a lot like those of early tetrapods, but they didn't seem terribly stiff. So, after doing the modeling, the lack of significant head mobility for almost all of these animals was a huge surprise.".

The findings suggest that the first animals with distinct necks could not simply turn their heads to survey their surroundings the way many modern land animals can.

Their ability to lift their heads was also extremely limited, sometimes falling below what would be expected in fish.

"Head elevation in these animals was no more than what you would expect in fish and, sometimes, even less," Korneisel noted. "We found that the kind of head twisting that we can do when we shake our heads was not feasible in any of these animals.".

The researchers also cautioned that their estimates may actually overstate how much movement was possible.

Their models considered the mechanical properties of the backbone itself, but other structures would have added further restrictions. Muscles, skin, and even bones embedded within the skin of some early tetrapods may have made their necks still more rigid.

Necks May Have Evolved for Walking Before Looking.

Together, the findings point to a different explanation for the origin of the neck.

Instead of first appearing because animals needed to turn their heads, the separation of the skull and shoulders may have developed alongside anatomical changes that allowed the front limbs to support and move the body.

In other words, the earliest necks may have been a consequence of adaptations for locomotion rather than an adaptation for improved vision or head movement.

According to recent reports, greater neck flexibility eventually evolved and became an important advantage for land vertebrates. But the latest evidence suggests that this benefit came later, after the basic structure of the neck was already established.

According to recent reports, the discovery also highlights the importance of the notochord in understanding animal evolution. Backbones dominated by this structure are uncommon among living vertebrates, but they were widespread during much of Earth's history. Studying modern animals that retain similar anatomy can therefore help scientists reconstruct how extinct creatures moved and behaved.

"We want to understand how these early tetrapods were living and how that is reflected in changes to their bodies," Stewart said. "Trying to reconstruct where an animal lived, how it moved, what its behavior was, is a really difficult thing. The cool part of this story is that it combines data from fossils and studies of living animals in a mechanical, functional perspective to reconstruct what the changes we see in the animal's anatomy mean for their behavior.".

By bringing together fossil discoveries, experiments on living fish, and biomechanical modeling, the researchers have challenged a familiar explanation for an anatomical feature that remains central to the bodies of humans and many other vertebrates today.

Sources indicate that along with Stewart and Korneisel, the international research team included Cassandra M. Donatelli of the University of Washington; Linfang Han, Marcos Martinez, Tetsuto Miyashita, and Emily M. Standen of the University of Ottawa in Canada; and Andrew L. Traynor, Benjamin K. A. Otoo, and Hillary C. Maddin of Carleton University in Canada.

The research received support from The Steven Cohen Award for Student Research, presented by the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology, and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (RGPIN-06442). The authors are solely responsible for the content, which does not necessarily reflect the views of the funding organizations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Children's clothing retailer The Children's Place has filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, it said Sunday.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer is looking to sell substantially all of its assets and is seeking offers from potential buyers by Dec. 9, with a goal to close a deal by the end of December.

According to recent reports, the retailer, whose brands include The Children's Place and Gymboree, indicates it operates two digital storefronts and 514 North American stores, and has distribution in 13 countries through franchise and wholesale partners. The tech giant's performance has taken a hit in recent years from tariff hikes and slower consumer spending, among other factors.

Its stores and e-commerce sites remain open for now, and the company is planning to continue its ongoing inventory sales with court approval.

In a recent development, "For nearly 60 years, The Children's Place has supported growing families with apparel that customers have come to know and love. We recognize the significance of this development for our employees, customers, vendors, and other partners, and we are committed to conducting an efficient and transparent sale process," mentioned Rudy Morando, co-chief restructuring officer of The Children's Place. "In the meantime, we remain focused on serving the families who have trusted The Children's Place for generations.".

This move comes days after interim Children's Place CEO Muhammad Asif Seemab and Chief Strategy Officer Muhammad Umair stepped down from their roles. Seemab and Umair will both remain on the company's board. CFO John Szczepanski took on the role of acting president and principal executive officer.

Seemab is also managing director of Saudi-based Mithaq Capital, which took a majority stake in The Children's Place in 2024 when the manufacturer was facing financial trouble.

Recent findings suggest that even with support from the investors, the company has not been able to significantly improve its financial outlook. In its bankruptcy filing, the company reported about $742 million in assets, compared to about $881 million in debts.

In the second fiscal quarter of 2026, its most recently reported quarter, the tech giant's net sales dropped nearly 19% from the same period the year prior. At the time, Seemab stated in a news release that during the quarter the company was "stabilizing our customer file" and "driving traffic to our stores and websites," and saw "lower conversion, combined with a very clearance-heavy mix.".

It has been revealed that he also pointed to tough comparisons to the prior-year period, due in part to back-to-school shopping demand that "was uniquely elevated ... ahead of anticipated tariff price increases.".

The Children's Place stock has plummeted in recent years and was trading around 18 cents per share on Monday.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI data centres have massive electricity demands, which are estimated to quadruple over the next decade.Credit: Mario Tama/Getty.
  • Ten countries including Germany and Brazil at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, have pledged to do more to limit the greenhouse-gas emissions produced by the rapid development of artificial intelligence — and to use the technology to cut emissions elsewhere.
  • According to recent reports, how much energy will AI really consume?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI data centres have massive electricity demands, which are estimated to quadruple over the next decade.Credit: Mario Tama/Getty.

Ten countries including Germany and Brazil at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, have pledged to do more to limit the greenhouse-gas emissions produced by the rapid development of artificial intelligence — and to use the technology to cut emissions elsewhere.

According to recent reports, how much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown.

“The pledge brings together two priorities that must advance together: reducing the environmental footprint of AI and expanding its contribution to climate action,” said Mehmet Fatih Kacır, Turkey’s minister of industry and technology at a launch event for the Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge on 16 November.

In a recent development, some climate advocates welcomed the pledge as a necessary, if vague, step to address the growing emissions and environmental impacts caused by running AI data centres. And researchers say there are ways that the technology could be used to cut emissions, for instance by helping to integrate renewables onto power grids or by improving logistics.

But it remains unknown whether such emissions reductions could offset AI’s consequences for the climate. “The trillion-dollar question is whether or not those savings will outweigh those impacts we’re seeing now,” indicates Eric Masanet, a mechanical engineer who studies decarbonization at the University of California, Santa Barbara.

The rapid building of AI data centres — which are used to train and operate AI systems — has drawn increasing ire from environmental quarters because of its insatiable demand for electricity. A report this month from BloombergNEF, which provides research on the clean-energy transition, estimated that electricity demand from data centres will quadruple over the next decade, making up 7% of global electricity demand in 2035, and accounting for at least 2% of global emissions.

According to recent reports, most of that would come from the United States, where the building of data-centres has been biggest and fastest, followed by China. In the race to train the most capable models, many substantial tech firms in the United States are seeking to build gas-fired power plants to satisfy data centres’ energy demands, rather than waiting for permission to connect to the public power grid.

Can AI models reliably forecast extreme weather events?

Can AI models reliably forecast extreme weather events?

That’s the sort of approach the pledge aims to prevent. It calls on countries to take action to power AI infrastructure with “zero- and low-emissions energy” and to improve the efficiency with which data centres use power and water for cooling. Countries that join will assess progress yearly.

It has been revealed that the other G20 countries that signed on are South Korea and Turkey, which sponsored the pledge and said it would aim to power its data centres with 60% low-carbon sources. They were initially joined by Andorra, Colombia, Luxembourg, Sierra Leone, Somalia and Uganda. More than 80 organizations endorsed the pledge, including a few large tech companies such as Nokia and Telefónica, according to a tracker from the UN’s International Telecommunications Union, one of the effort’s organizing bodies. However, none of the frontier AI firms have joined the pledge.

Sources indicate that given the absence of AI’s biggest emitters, some climate advocates dismissed the initiative. “The AI pledge risks giving Major Tech a green stamp without requiring it to address the real climate impacts of its infrastructure,” says Jill McArdle, a campaigner at Beyond Fossil Fuels, an advocacy group in Berlin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So many people are dying of Ebola that their bodies have been stacked, one atop the other, on makeshift racks in a shed by the hospital gate.

The town’s main cemetery is full, so fresh graves are being squeezed in between palm trees by the side of the road.

Medicine, IVs and basic protections have been so scarce that three-quarters of Ebola patients in this besieged Congolese town have died.

Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province.

It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as it moves through one of the world’s great rainforests.

Instead of one massive fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain.

In a recent development, health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of newly introduced cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

Recent findings suggest that “We see the same mistakes as before,” noted Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.”.

And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The documentary, entitled Spirit of the Photobooth, played an encore screening at the International Center of Photography Saturday as part of the inaugural Art Week from Artforum and ARTnews.
  • As told in the film, Anatol Josepho, a Russian immigrant to the U.S., founded the automated analog photobooth as a means for everyday people to be able to get their own portraits, instead of the more expensive and time intensive process of sitting for a studio photo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In honor of the 100th anniversary of the humble photobooth, a new documentary unveils its democratic origins, its place in history as means of self-expression and its recent resurgence among Gen-Z.

The documentary, entitled Spirit of the Photobooth, played an encore screening at the International Center of Photography Saturday as part of the inaugural Art Week from Artforum and ARTnews. The film, written and directed by Sam Anthony, first premiered in September.

As told in the film, Anatol Josepho, a Russian immigrant to the U.S., founded the automated analog photobooth as a means for everyday people to be able to get their own portraits, instead of the more expensive and time intensive process of sitting for a studio photo. The first photobooths were located just north of Times Square and caused a sensation in 1926, with crowds lining up for a chance in the booth until 4 a.m. The next year Josepho sold the patent for the booths for $1 million to businessman Henry Morgenthau, who debuted booths across the nation.

From there, photo booths popped up at army bases, allowing soldiers to send home a photo, and expanded into Europe, where they were favored among members of the surrealist movement. The automated, private nature of the booths also gave Black Americans a chance for self-expression in the Jim Crow South, and gave queer couples an opportunity to take home private keepsakes, with some photobooths stationed in men’s bathrooms. Andy Warhol used photobooth strips as a basis for his pop art and silk screen painting, helping to legitimize it as a form of art.

While photobooths gradually fell into disuse, due to the rise of digital cameras and cell phones with cameras, a dedicated group of enthusiasts across the globe have worked to bring old booths back to life — the refurbishment is pricey, but the business of booths is quickly profitable — and to revive enthusiasm for the practice.

Happily, Gen-Z has since flocked to photobooths — with one owner noting it may be “some of the only analog tech” they’ve experienced — as enthusiasts say they’re in search of something tangible and real, and have seen the locations promoted on social media.The Old Friend Photobooth in lower Manhattan is one of the most popular current locations, with the Gen-Z owners now turning their attention to refurbishing a booth at Coney Island, the former mecca for photo booths from the 1940s through ‘70s.

#608. Industry News: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1440 w)
