💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX released the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov.
  • Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m.
  • Recent findings suggest that the flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX released the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines.

Recent findings suggest that the flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO).

SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The manufacturer called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear.

A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy, which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The organization previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights.

Ship's Raptors continued to fire following stage separation, completing their first burn just after eight minutes into flight. All went according to blueprint after that for Ship as well: A second engine burn lasting about 20 seconds parked Ship in LEO at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) at T+26 minutes and 10 seconds.

"We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot noted during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment.".

Ship first reached orbit on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28.

Ship carried 26 of SpaceX's Starlink V3 spacecraft, which were deployed into LEO on schedule today over a 42-minute span starting 35 minutes after launch.

The upgraded wireless internet satellites are the second V3 batch to reach orbit, after a set of 26 that were delivered on Flight 14 . V3s are significantly more powerful than SpaceX's V2 Starlinks, which right now number more than 11,000 in LEO. The addition of this newly introduced set of V3s will add a terabit of data capacity to the constellation, according to SpaceX's Flight 15 mission outline. That's equivalent to the amount contributed by 10 Starlink V2 launches, which are carried out by SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket.

According to recent reports, three of the V3 Starlinks flying today were equipped with cameras to point back at Ship after deployment in order to analyze its heatshield tiles and other hardware following its ascent to orbit. Their data will help SpaceX determine if Ship can indeed come home to Starbase on Saturday.

"Starship will only execute a return to launch site if the flight control team has ensured that the vehicle systems critical for reentry maneuvers and final landing burn and tower approach are healthy," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.

SpaceX engineers will have ample time to go over Ship's systems before making a final landing decision. Ship is scheduled to circle Earth 14 times, spending more than 21 hours in space before coming home.

You can follow all of the action on here at Space.com via our Flight 15 live updates page.

Recent findings suggest that spaceX has reserved three contingency checkpoints during Flight 15's mission timeline to allow for an early Pacific Ocean return, should engineers determine a catch attempt to be unfeasible or unwise. The first comes just 10 minutes after the completion of Starlink satellite deployment, the second at T+7 hours and 15 minutes, and a final one at T+20 hours and 41 minutes.

Should Ship continue to look good through each of these milestones, SpaceX will proceed with a 10-second deorbit burn at approximately T+21 hours and 36 minutes, setting the spacecraft on a trajectory back toward South Texas. Its plunge through Earth's atmosphere will begin about 35 minutes later. SpaceX has also designated a contingency splashdown zone in the Gulf of Mexico, should conditions prevent a safe catch during Ship's final approach.

If all goes according to initiative, Ship will return to Starbase on Saturday at approximately 4:17 p.m. EST (2117 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Texas time), about 22.5 hours after liftoff. A successful catch would be a major milestone for SpaceX — the first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage.

Full reusability is central to the firm's ambitions for launching its V3 Starlink satellites, as well as a proposed constellation of orbital data centers envisioned by company founder and CEO Elon Musk. The next-gen Starlink constellation will consist of about 100,000 satellites, while the AI network will be 10 times that size, Musk has said. Building and maintaining those constellations will require a mind-boggling number of launches. Indeed, SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship liftoffs per year by 2030, according to Musk.

In a recent development, some of Starship's other planned missions won't necessarily require full reusability, but the spacecraft's reliability will be critical to NASA's Artemis program and its efforts to return astronauts to the moon. The space agency selected Starship as one of the program's crewed lunar landers, and it's slated to fly a demonstration mission with NASA's Orion spacecraft and Artemis III astronauts to Earth orbit in the summer of 2027.

NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans.
  • Sources indicate that unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state).
  • According to recent reports, scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans. But turbulence also occurs throughout space, where it behaves in ways that scientists are still struggling to understand.

Sources indicate that unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state). These particles interact strongly with magnetic and electric fields, creating turbulence that is fundamentally different from what we experience on Earth. Space plasma is also so thinly spread that particles rarely collide with one another, making its behavior even more unusual.

According to recent reports, scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations. Now, an international research team has uncovered a surprising clue: hidden within the seemingly random motion of space plasma is a distinct magnetic pattern that reverses direction at very small scales.

The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, reveals a previously unobserved phenomenon that could improve our understanding of the solar wind and the turbulent conditions that influence space weather.

NASA's Parker Solar Probe Reveals a Hidden Magnetic Reversal.

Researchers from the Technische Universität Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, working with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other international institutions, identified the phenomenon using observations from NASA's Parker Solar Probe.

The collaboration brought together scientists from ten countries, including researchers at the Institute of Theoretical Physics at Technische Universität Braunschweig.

Sources indicate that by analyzing highly precise measurements of magnetic fields and particles, the team discovered that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation at a particular range of wavelengths. This marks the first direct observation of such a reversal in space turbulence.

Even more surprisingly, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths as the solar wind travels farther from the Sun.

In a recent development, the change occurs at a critical boundary where the behavior of plasma shifts from the collective movement of a flowing fluid to the dynamics of individual particles. This connection suggests that the magnetic reversal may provide an vital new way to understand how turbulence operates across different physical scales.

Finding Order in the Chaos of Space Turbulence.

Recent findings suggest that at larger scales, plasma moves much like a fluid. Swirling structures called vortices and electromagnetic waves create increasingly complex fluctuations, producing the turbulent conditions found throughout space.

Although these movements appear random, the researchers discovered that the rotation of the magnetic fields follows a consistent pattern.

Industry observers note that when viewed along a direction pointing outward from the Sun, magnetic fields at larger scales tend to rotate counterclockwise. At much smaller scales, however, the preferred rotation switches to clockwise.

This reversal occurs precisely where plasma stops behaving primarily like a fluid and begins exhibiting behavior governed by individual particles.

The finding is particularly striking because it reveals a clear, organized feature within a system otherwise dominated by seemingly unpredictable fluctuations.

"We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions," says Dr. Masatomi Iizawa (TU Braunschweig), the study's first author.

Dr. Yokoi (University. of Tokyo) emphasizes the broader importance of the discovery, stating, "The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics.".

Why the Discovery Matters for Solar Storms and Space Weather.

Although the magnetic reversal occurs at extremely small scales, understanding it could have far-reaching consequences for space physics.

Plasma turbulence is a major feature of many environments throughout the universe, including Earth's magnetosphere, the solar wind, regions affected by solar eruptions, interplanetary space, and the disks of material surrounding astronomical objects known as accretion disks.

It also influences the shock waves and clouds of magnetic material that travel through interplanetary space following eruptions on the Sun.

These disturbances can play an key role in geomagnetic storms, making plasma turbulence a critical factor in efforts to predict space weather.

Sources indicate that by showing how an organized magnetic pattern emerges as turbulent plasma transitions from fluid behavior to particle behavior, the new research provides an notable piece of a longstanding physics puzzle. The findings could ultimately help scientists better understand the complex processes that govern the solar wind and improve the physical models used to forecast geomagnetic storms.

The psychology of imaginary friends — and why they are good for kids

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Projecting thoughts and feelings onto imagined friends helps children to develop their social skills.Credit: Oscar Wong/Getty.
  • In a recent development, the Imagination Scientist: Researching Pretend Beings and their Creators Paige E.
  • When my brother Arnie was about four years old, he began chatting about an imaginary and invisible companion named Embley, who seemingly travelled with him everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Projecting thoughts and feelings onto imagined friends helps children to develop their social skills.Credit: Oscar Wong/Getty.

In a recent development, the Imagination Scientist: Researching Pretend Beings and their Creators Paige E. Davis Oxford Univ. Press (2026).

When my brother Arnie was about four years old, he began chatting about an imaginary and invisible companion named Embley, who seemingly travelled with him everywhere. During a 1970s epidemic of whooping cough (linked to an unwarranted vaccine-safety scare), Arnie became sick with this braying cough, which kept him home from school for more than six weeks.

Embley was the “same size, age and disposition as me”, my brother recalled later, and he offered companionship and “exploration of potential sources of adventure”. Although he could not remember other aspects of Embley’s personality or appearance, my brother did add one pertinent detail: “He was always available.”.

The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?

The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?

I thought of Embley while reading The Imagination Scientist, a deeply researched and highly entertaining look at the world of imaginary companions by developmental psychologist Paige Davis.

It seems that Embley exemplified several features of children’s imaginary friends: he was comforting and constant; he played with my brother; and he perhaps enabled him to process fear and cope with the stress of a serious illness. He might also have insulated my brother from loneliness while his older siblings were at school. Most importantly, my brother himself created Embley’s mind.

Industry observers note that that last characteristic of an imaginary friend is key, asserts Davis. “My theory is that the most notable aspect of the imaginary creature, no matter whether it is seen or unseen, lies in the creation of its mind by the child,” she writes. “To have an invisible friend or personified object considered as an imaginary companion, the child must create, conceptualize, and interact with the separate and distinct mind.”.

Davis opens a wardrobe door, Narnia-style, into a whimsical world inhabited by imaginary companions — some invisible, others personified in a doll or stuffed toy. Up to 65% of children up to the age of seven have had imaginary companions at some stage, according to research by psychologist Marjorie Taylor. Some imaginary friends disappear at the end of childhood, others continue to accompany their creators into adolescence. But not all made-up playmates are friendly: some are a nuisance and might even pick fights with their creators (or vice versa).

Sources indicate that generally, there’s nothing pathological about creating a pretend friend, Davis contends. On the contrary, the presence of such a pal might fortify the child as they deal with transitions or scary situations. Children do understand the distinction between fantasy friends and real ones, and can grasp this difference as young as three years old. “Imaginary friends are a very common, developmentally appropriate phenomena that occurs in multiple cultures around the world,” Davis writes. They “are not only a healthy form of play, but they can be extremely enjoyable for their creator”.

Imaginary friends can offer a child a sense of protection.Credit: Ian Nolan/Getty.

They’re also great fun to read about. I laughed aloud as I learnt about some of the “human, non-human, and superhuman” forms that Davis has encountered while interviewing children for her research. “I’ve had blue blobs, yellow birds, and rainbow hair,” she writes, “a fire-boy who erupts like a volcano when he becomes angry” and “a genderless imaginary companion that snacks on lightbulbs”. One little girl had twin imaginary companions, who themselves had made their own imaginary friend, “which I thought was quite meta”, she writes.

Davis first began immersing herself in the world of imaginary companions as a PhD student at the University of Durham, UK. I “thought about how much fun it would be to work with children, play, and imagination for a job”, Davis writes. Skydance is pulling back the curtain on how it aims to achieve at least $6 billion in cost savings in the next three years.

"By combining two global streaming services, two film and TV studio groups, two television portfolios, and overlapping corporate functions, we can reduce duplicative spend across an expense base of more than $50 billion," the tech giant wrote in a letter to shareholders Monday as part of Paramount Skydance's third-quarter earnings release.

According to recent reports, skydance, the organization formed by the combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, said it projects at least $2.2 billion in cost reductions from eliminating "redundant back-office and corporate functions," including eliminating management layers and ramping the use of artificial intelligence. Those savings also account for "rationalizing" its office footprint.

In a recent development, skydance expects at least $1 billion in savings from streamlining marketing and promotional spending. And around $1.4 billion in savings will come from unifying its streaming businesses and broadcast architecture and integrating back-end technology.

A final $1.4 billion in savings will be tied to "optimizing third-party spend," eliminating overlapping expenses, and consolidating purchasing decisions to one centralized group, Skydance noted.

According to recent reports, "We are confident in achieving these savings, drawing on our playbook from Paramount," the organization wrote. "That program is on track to achieve over $2.7 billion in run-rate efficiencies by the end of 2026.".

Some of that cost-cutting has already begun.

In a recent development, last month, Skydance began offering voluntary buyouts to employees ahead of official layoffs. At the same time, the manufacturer adopted a five-day-per-week in-office policy. Additionally, last week saw the departure of eight executives — four from Warner Bros. and four from Paramount.

The organization has previously said it plans to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services into a single platform.

On Monday, Skydance noted it would take the first step toward that goal early next year, offering a bundle of the streaming services "at an even greater value.".

Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told investors during the firm's earnings call that Skydance is also looking for ways to optimize its content budget. The company spends more than $30 billion annually on shows and films.

"As one tech giant, we can make smarter choices about how we distribute and monetize both new content and library content," Kreiz mentioned.

Sources indicate that skydance noted that it's expecting a $200 million headwind in the fourth quarter from theatrical underperformances at Warner Bros. studio related to already released titles and upcoming releases.

The tech giant will also utilize AI to speed up production and decrease costs to make films, co-CEO and chairman David Ellison said on the call.

"We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budget more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk," Ellison said.

The updates came alongside third-quarter results for the legacy Paramount Skydance tech giant that included revenue of $7.03 billion, which was roughly in line with StreetAccount estimates of $7.04 billion, and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $1 billion, topping StreetAccount estimates of $913.5 million.

However, adjusted earnings per share of 45 cents were not immediately comparable to StreetAccount EPS estimates.

Sources indicate that the results don't include the impact of the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, which closed after the end of the third quarter.

Skydance detailed business units of the combined entity, including studios, direct-to-consumer and TV, and noted it will provide full-year guidance during its fourth-quarter earnings report early next year.

"Going forward, we will provide guidance on an annual basis, as we prioritize long-term value creation, which we believe will be more consistent with our strategic approach," the tech giant told shareholders. "We will continue to provide quarterly updates, including certain forward-looking commentary where applicable, which will give investors visibility into our near-term progress of the business.".

#573. The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (805 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow.
  • Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery.
  • The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth.

Sources indicate that for laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a upcoming placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

It has been revealed that as the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. New placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation.

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

According to recent reports, chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

The researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

Remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

"Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals.".

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns.

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

They selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

The results showed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

Sources indicate that these findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

Recent findings suggest that "Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals.".

Microsoft remarked early Saturday that it had fully restored its services after a global outage disrupted them for a day and a half, hampering communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world.

The problems began on Thursday and cascaded around the world. The organization, based in Redmond, Wash., gradually restored service through Friday until declaring an end to one of its most extensive outages of recent times in an enhancement on Saturday around 1 a.m. Eastern time.

Outages started disrupting Microsoft tools and apps around noon Eastern time on Thursday and quickly spread to more than 70 countries and territories, affecting millions of owners, according to Downdetector, an outage-tracking site.

Some of Microsoft’s most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, stopped working.

Microsoft mentioned in a statement on Friday that “for now, we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” It added that the problem was “a technical issue not related to cyber or A.I.” agents.

The manufacturer said it had no indication that a Federal Aviation Administration ground stop issued late Friday afternoon, which has affected air travel nationwide, was related to the outage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029.

Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky.

It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth.

The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years, when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse.

Recent findings suggest that both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus, which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun.

A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant, formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams.

Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA.

Recent findings suggest that interested in seeing and capturing the planets for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide on everything you need to observe and photograph the planets of the solar system, along with our picks of the top telescopes, cameras and lenses for exploring the night sky in 2026.

#567. Latest Update: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

Latest Update: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered latest clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels.
  • Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death.
  • Reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered latest clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

Reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an key role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," notes Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

Cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

In a recent development, these plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form rapidly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol.".

Sources indicate that to investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

All three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

Industry observers note that the researchers also identified two particularly important contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

Recent findings suggest that while genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Industry observers note that because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks.

The latest investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

It has been revealed that researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns indicated substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

The researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

It has been revealed that LDL showed a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an important distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

In a recent development, "The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," says Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future.".

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health.

According to recent reports, the three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

All three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

In a recent development, LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

It has been revealed that TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an key energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

Recent findings suggest that lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

According to recent reports, by identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers upcoming possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

According to recent reports, however, the research did not evaluate a latest treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

In a recent development, "Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," claims Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments.".

Industry observers note that the results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

Study Details and Research Institutions.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

It has been revealed that at the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.

Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.
  • Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.
  • His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, confirmed his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, confirmed his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Recent findings suggest that using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

According to recent reports, “You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

Recent findings suggest that by the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The Fresh Yorker.

It has been revealed that T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

Top image: Kwame Brathwaite, “Untitled (Sikolo Brathwaite, Orange Portrait),” 1968.

Breaking: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An ancient rodent of extraordinary size has been identified from fossils uncovered in a mine in southern Thailand.
  • It has been revealed that the researchers found "remarkably large" fossilized teeth belonging to a previously unknown species called Yakamys sirindhornae.
  • Industry observers note that although only two teeth have been identified, they offer valuable clues about rodent gigantism, the evolutionary process through which rodents develop unusually large bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An ancient rodent of extraordinary size has been identified from fossils uncovered in a mine in southern Thailand. The discovery, made by an international team of paleontologists that includes scientists from McGill University, provides new evidence that giant rodents appeared much earlier and in more parts of the world than previously believed.

It has been revealed that the researchers found "remarkably large" fossilized teeth belonging to a previously unknown species called Yakamys sirindhornae. This prehistoric rodent lived approximately 34 million years ago, during the middle of the Paleogene period. Its remains, consisting of a lower second molar and a lower incisor, were recovered from the Bang Mark Pit at the Krabi lignite mine in Thailand's Krabi Province.

Industry observers note that although only two teeth have been identified, they offer valuable clues about rodent gigantism, the evolutionary process through which rodents develop unusually large bodies. The discovery suggests that Southeast Asia played a more significant role in the early evolution of giant rodents than scientists had recognized.

Giant Rodents Have a Much Older History Than Expected.

In a recent development, "Today, the largest living rodent is the capybara, but very large rodents are not restricted to recent ecosystems," remarked Virginie Millien, a biology professor at McGill University and co-author of the study. "Giant rodents evolved repeatedly during the later history of the group, mostly in South America. This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an vital role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents.".

The newly identified animal's name reflects both its impressive size and its connection to Thailand. Yakamys combines "yak," the Thai word for giant, with "mys," the Greek word for mouse or rat.

The second part of its scientific name recognizes an important supporter of scientific research in Thailand.

"The species name, sirindhornae, honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her longstanding support for science and paleontological research in Thailand," Millien mentioned.

How Major Was This 34-Million-Year-Old Rodent?

Recent findings suggest that to estimate the animal's size, the research team applied seven established methods that use tooth measurements to calculate body mass. Their results suggest that Yakamys sirindhornae weighed approximately 30 kilograms, making it about twice as heavy as other known rodents from the same period, including Hulgana.

That would have made the newly discovered species exceptionally large compared with its contemporaries. However, the researchers emphasize that determining an extinct animal's weight from a small number of fossilized teeth involves considerable uncertainty.

"This is only a ballpark figure, as there is substantial uncertainty associated with fossil body-mass estimation," Millien remarked.

The limited fossil evidence also makes it difficult to reconstruct how Yakamys evolved or what its life was like. Additional discoveries will be needed to better understand its physical characteristics, ecological role, and evolutionary relationships.

International Research Uncovers Thailand's Prehistoric Past.

Industry observers note that the fossils were identified through an ongoing international collaboration investigating ancient mammals in Thailand's Krabi Basin. The project brings together scientists from McGill University, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, and French research organizations, including CNRS and Université de Poitiers.

By revealing evidence of an unusually large rodent in Southeast Asia 34 million years ago, the discovery expands scientists' understanding of where and when rodent gigantism emerged. Future fossil finds could help establish how these ancient giants lived and how their evolution relates to the enormous rodents that appeared elsewhere in the world.

The research received support from CNRS, Université de Poitiers, Université de Montpellier, McGill University, and the Department of Mineral Resources of Thailand.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov.
  • Industry observers note that starship released on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that that didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.

Industry observers note that starship released on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission initiative called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket.

Recent findings suggest that that didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse.

"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast today, his voice thick with emotion. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes.".

Sources indicate that the Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off.

Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the manufacturer calls "Mechazilla.".

And they got quite a show: Ship 42 nestled gently into Mechazilla's waiting arms, while "Baby Come Back" played over SpaceX's landing webcast.

According to recent reports, "This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson remarked during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes.".

According to recent reports, why was this such a massive deal? SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy — on three previous Starship test flights, in fact. But it had never tried before with Ship. The upper stage is a tougher target, for it flies higher, farther and faster than the booster. Indeed, on Flight 15, Ship 42 came all the way back down from orbit.

While the double-catch attempt, and the chopsticks success with Ship, were Flight 15's main headlines, the mission had other objectives as well. One was getting Ship to orbit, which had happened on just one previous Starship launch — Flight 14, which lifted off on Sept. 28.

Ship deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) on Flight 14, and it did so again on Flight 15. These 52 spacecraft are the first members of a constellation that will eventually consist of 100,000 satellites, if all goes according to SpaceX's plan.

Recent findings suggest that some of those Starlink satellites took video and images of Ship 42's heat shield to check its health for today's landing attempt. Those images, combined with ground-based cameras, found Ship 42 to be in good shape and ready for its major moment.

SpaceX plans to use Starship to build an even bigger network in LEO than the Starlink V3 system — Starmind, an AI data-center constellation that will harbor a million spacecraft, according to Elon Musk. (For context: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network employs about 11,000 satellites at the moment.).

Assembling these megaconstellations will require an incredible launch cadence. The double chopstick catch is key to that vision, SpaceX says, for it will enable quicker inspection, refurbishment and reflight of Starship.

So the company will doubtless try the maneuver again soon — probably on the next Starship flight, which won't be too far down the road.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A squabble over the publication timetable for several climate reports has turned into one of the burning concerns of this year’s United Nations climate conference, as some warn that fossil fuel interests might be interfering with the world’s pre-eminent climate science organization.

The U.N.-backed Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change produces landmark reports that generally come out every five to seven years. The next round of reports would take on topics like physical changes to the earth and greenhouse gas emissions.

Timing is critical because in 2028 nations are supposed to assess their progress and then ramp up their efforts to do more, based on the best science. That process, known as a stocktake and occurring every five years, is the engine of the Paris Agreement.

Saudi Arabia, India and Russia are among those pushing to delay the reports so that at least two of them come out after 2028.

The fact that those nations rank among the largest fossil fuel exporters or importers has led to accusations that coal, oil and gas interests might be interfering with science.

“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the I.P.C.C. in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” said former Vice President Al Gore, who is in Turkey for the talks.

#560. Breaking: In Choosing Robert Pattinson, Bond Producers Have Taken the Safe Bet — But Is It the Right One? (Opinion)

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (953 w)
📖 Baca

Breaking: In Choosing Robert Pattinson, Bond Producers Have Taken the Safe Bet — But Is It the Right One? (Opinion)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The star of 'The Drama' and 'The Odyssey' caps off a massive year by winning the highest-profile casting contest in ages, but it's hard not to wonder if he really needs this.
  • After the race to be the next James Bond was reported to be down to three on-the-rise Brits — Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner — Robert Pattinson crashed the conversation late in proceedings, hugely pulling focus in a matter of days.
  • In a recent development, why wouldn’t he?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The star of 'The Drama' and 'The Odyssey' caps off a massive year by winning the highest-profile casting contest in ages, but it's hard not to wonder if he really needs this.

So much for the underdog. After the race to be the next James Bond was reported to be down to three on-the-rise Brits — Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner — Robert Pattinson crashed the conversation late in proceedings, hugely pulling focus in a matter of days.

In a recent development, why wouldn’t he? Suddenly, a competition of next-substantial-things had a bona fide already-big-thing in the mix. 40 years old and known to multiplex audiences for almost half that lifetime, the Londoner is a household name who, even by his established standards, has been enjoying a banner year at the movies: sharing in the blockbuster glory of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” this summer, sandwiched by inspired star turns in two offbeat A24 projects, “The Drama” and “Primetime,” that both impressively overperformed at the box office. All that, and he’s still got “Dune: Part Three” coming up next month. Related Stories Paul Bettany, Asha Banks, Gugu Mbatha-Raw and Colin Firth Team for Feel-Good Comedy 'It's Alright,' Protagonist Launches Sales at AFM (EXCLUSIVE) Keira Knightley Indicates ‘It Means Nothing' When Fans Quote ‘Love Actually’ to Her Because She Hasn’t Watched It Since the Premiere: ‘I Don’t Remember It’.

Adding James Bond to his roster feels almost like gilding the lily, which is one reason I was skeptical that he’d ultimately be picked: Wasn’t the announcement of Pattinson (along with Nicholas Hoult) as a contender just a glittery distraction to juice up public interest in a lower-profile selection process?

Indicates what I know. In picking Pattinson as the next 007, the 64-year-old movie franchise is heading into unprecedented territory: Bond has traditionally been a star-making role, not one for a readymade movie star, and that has worked out more often than not. (George Lazenby, it simply wasn’t meant to be.) Sean Connery had played just one leading role before he was cast in 1962’s “Dr. No”; prior to donning the tux, Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan had both found their signature roles on TV. Timothy Dalton, a reasonably seasoned and well-regarded actor when cast as Bond, never quite made the leap to stardom via the role; Daniel Craig, on the other hand, very much did.

Lowden, Turner and O’Connor all made perfect sense given this history, while Pattinson, already known to billions for playing Edward Cullen and Batman, brings associative celebrity baggage that Bond has never had to contend with before. Is that a problem? Not necessarily. Director Denis Villeneuve, a high-end, blue-chip blockbuster artist with a distinct stylistic signature, isn’t the typical choice of Bond helmer either — so if he’s going in his own prestigious direction with the series, it makes sense for him to take an equivalently A-list leading man (and one with whom he has an existing relationship, through “Dune: Part Three”) with him.

And yet there’s something about the choice, on paper at least, that doesn’t sit right with me. It seems a little too neat, too convenient, even a bit too risk-averse — the proven safe bet taken over the chance to mint a brand-new megastar. I have little doubt that Pattinson, a reliably terrific actor, will make a fine Bond: tall and elegant and angularly handsome, he certainly looks the part and he can project the balance of charm and chill needed to play a character who, in any incarnation, remains a suave killing machine.

Is he a little too good for the part, though? Perhaps. Pattinson’s reputation as a movie star rests on playing two darkly brooding mainstream heroes; his reputation as an actor, however, has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos: a hapless small-time criminal in the Safdie Brothers’ “Good Time”; a deranged, gull-mauling lighthouse keeper in “The Lighthouse”; a sniveling, pathetic read of Chris Hansen in “Primetime”; or whatever the hell he’s doing, multiple times over, in Bong Joon-ho’s loopy sci-fi “Mickey 17.” Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play: His major, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in “The Odyssey” is off on its own beam entirely.

Industry observers note that I don’t know that James Bond is really the role to mine Pattinson’s most compelling eccentricities as an actor: The very point of the character, across 25 films, has been that he’s a well-dressed, tightly controlled cipher who has a sharp way with a one-liner. Perhaps Villeneuve and his chosen star have other ideas, but it’s hard to imagine the character straying too far from a failsafe template. One hopes instead that Pattinson is negotiating himself enough time between 007 shoots (and at least one more “The Batman” entry still on the docket) to do the odd auteur projects he clearly loves — and that adventurously chosen collaborators like Claire Denis (“High Life”) and Lynne Ramsay (“Die My Love”) can only benefit from his cachet.

In the meantime, spare a thought for the less famous guys who, for a moment there, thought they had a shot at being cinema’s longest-running action man. They’ll all be fine — I confess to some relief in particular that O’Connor, a superb and unusual hybrid of character actor and leading man, may have more time for the intrepid arthouse projects in which he thrives — and will doubtless each get some manner of boost for having been so prominently on the shortlist. Sometimes, however, the winner really does take it all in this business: For Pattinson, snagging the most in-demand role going just feels like a victory lap.

#558. A massive upcoming simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

A massive upcoming simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.
  • Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide.
  • The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.

Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide. It follows 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how galaxies formed, how radiation spread through space, and how the universe gradually became transparent to light.

The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.

How the Universe Entered Its Cosmic Dark Age.

In a recent development, the story begins with the Significant Bang, when the universe existed in an extremely hot, dense state filled with electrons and other subatomic particles. This primordial plasma, described as initially smaller than a single atom, expanded rapidly and cooled as the universe grew.

According to recent reports, eventually, particles slowed enough for electrons to combine with atomic nuclei, producing electrically neutral hydrogen. Around 380,000 years after the Major Bang, the universe entered a period known as the cosmic "dark age.".

Although the universe had become transparent to much of the radiation left over from the Significant Bang, stars had not yet formed to illuminate the cosmos. Neutral hydrogen filled space and could absorb certain types of radiation, including the ultraviolet light that would later emerge from the first stars.

Lumina allows researchers to investigate how this early environment evolved, eventually giving rise to the galaxies, stars, and other structures that helped bring the dark age to an end.

How the First Stars and Black Holes Transformed the Universe.

Recent findings suggest that the simulation covers an immense region measuring 500 megaparsecs, equivalent to approximately 1.6 billion light-years. Within that volume, Lumina follows dark matter, gas, stars, and radiation (such as photons), capturing both the behavior of matter across enormous distances and the formation of individual galaxies.

One of its most crucial achievements is recreating two major changes in the early universe: hydrogen re-ionization and helium re-ionization.

Hydrogen re-ionization began as the first stars and galaxies produced increasing amounts of ultraviolet radiation. This energetic light removed electrons from neutral hydrogen atoms, a process called "re-ionizing" the gas. As more hydrogen became ionized, the universe became increasingly transparent to ultraviolet light, allowing radiation to travel across much greater distances.

Recent findings suggest that this transformation helped clear the widespread neutral hydrogen that had dominated the early cosmos. Lumina reproduces the process in remarkable detail, showing how radiation from the first generations of stars gradually changed the conditions throughout space.

The simulation also follows helium re-ionization, which requires substantially more energetic radiation to strip electrons from helium.

The results point to different sources driving these two transformations. Early stars and galaxies appear to have been primarily responsible for ionizing hydrogen, while actively feeding supermassive black holes supplied the intense radiation needed to ionize helium.

This is the first simulation to capture both processes together, offering a more complete view of how the early universe changed.

"Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale reionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations," says study author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers are making Lumina available to other scientists, allowing its predictions about early cosmic structures to be compared with observations from existing and future telescopes. Such comparisons could help researchers better understand the events that shaped the first galaxies and stars.

Building a Virtual Universe With Half a Trillion Elements.

Lumina gets its name from the Latin word meaning "lights." Its underlying technology builds on IllustrisTNG, an earlier simulation developed by scientists at MIT and other institutions, including members of the Lumina research team.

IllustrisTNG models how galaxies form and evolve by following the interactions of dark matter, gas, and other physical processes from the Significant Bang to the present day.

It has been revealed that to create Lumina, researchers upgraded the existing software so it could reproduce galaxy formation in comparable detail across a much larger region of space. They also incorporated a radiation transport model that calculates how light, including ultraviolet radiation, travels through the universe and interacts with surrounding matter.

Together, these improvements allow the simulation to track both the formation of galaxies and the enormous changes that radiation produces across cosmic distances.

The resulting model contains approximately half a trillion individual elements, including particles of dark matter and cells representing gas. It provides roughly 30 times the resolution of IllustrisTNG while covering a region 100 times larger in volume than previous leading simulations.

Recreating billions of years of interactions across so many elements requires extraordinary computing resources. The researchers used Frontier, one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, located at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

Recent findings suggest that "At peak scale, the calculation brings together the equivalent of more than 100,000 CPU cores and around 15,000 GPUs," says Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, an MIT co-author of the study. "Making all of those processors communicate efficiently while continuously evolving trillions of interacting pieces of information is itself an extraordinary feat of computer engineering.".

Watching the First Galaxies Emerge From Darkness.

Lumina begins approximately 45 million years after the Big Bang, during an era when neutral hydrogen dominated the universe.

Researchers initialized the simulation using conditions based on scientists' understanding of that period. They then allowed the model to calculate how gas and dark matter interacted throughout its half a trillion elements as cosmic time progressed.

At the same time, Lumina tracked how radiation appeared, spread, and interacted with matter, including the ultraviolet light produced by emerging stars.

The result is a virtual universe that scientists can explore at dramatically different scales, from the arrangement of matter across enormous cosmic distances down to the development of a single galaxy.

Recent findings suggest that on the project website, the researchers have released videos showing these processes in action. One offers a "zoom-in" from the entire simulated region to an individual disk-shaped galaxy. Another presents a time-lapse of the complete volume, showing how hydrogen re-ionization spreads across the universe over 2 billion years.

Recent findings suggest that "On the one hand, it's evolving dark matter as well as the gas in the universe, and on the other, it's also tracking how radiation travels," Zier explains. "We see dark matter and gas start to clump in these over-densities. And when we zoom in, we can see gas is falling into these dark matter haloes. Zooming in more, we see this is where the first galaxies form. And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen.".

This ability to move between vastly different scales is one of Lumina's defining strengths. Researchers can examine the formation of individual galaxies while also observing how their combined radiation affects the universe on a much larger scale.

Industry observers note that "Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," Vogelsberger notes. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation.".

A New Way to Explore the Universe's Earliest History.

The research team aims to use Lumina to investigate the large-scale arrangement of matter in the early universe. The simulation could also help predict the patterns of gravitational waves generated by ancient galaxies and black holes.

Another major opportunity will come from comparing Lumina's virtual universe with real observations. Fresh and upcoming telescopes are expected to collect increasingly detailed information about enormous numbers of distant galaxies, providing scientists with fresh ways to test their understanding of the early cosmos.

Because Lumina simulates such a large volume of space, it can generate extensive populations of galaxies that can be directly compared with these observations.

In a recent development, "One of Lumina's major advantages is its sheer size," Shen states. "It produces enormous populations of simulated galaxies, finally allowing us to make comparisons with the very large galaxy samples that upcoming surveys will observe.".

By bringing together detailed galaxy formation, dark matter, gas, and the movement of radiation, Lumina offers researchers a powerful new tool for reconstructing the universe's earliest chapters. It may help explain not only how the first galaxies took shape, but also how their stars and black holes transformed the surrounding cosmos.

The study's MIT authors include Mark Vogelsberger, Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, and Teodora-Elena Bluichi. Other contributors include first author Oliver Zier (a former postdoc in the Vogelsberger Lab), Rongrong Liu, Sonja Koehler, and Lars Hernquist of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics; Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas; Rahul Kannan of York University in Canada; and Volker Springel and Rüdiger Pakmor of the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics in Germany.

The research received partial support from NASA and the National Science Foundation. It also used computing resources at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which is supported by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research programs within the Office of Science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed
